newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hurt by weak U.S. assets, German rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hurt by weak U.S. assets, German rate hike fears.

text.p: The dollar tumbled against the mark Friday, hurt by a sharp fall in U.S. stocks and mounting speculation that Germany will raise interest rates.
The dollar also fell against the yen, but losses were limited amid lingering concerns that recent Southeast Asian currency devaluations would undermine the Japanese currency.

The dollar fell more than two pfennigs, trading below 1.82 marks for the first time in three weeks, as many investors liquidated dollars and dollar-denominated investments, fearing the recent bull run has come to an end.

"The tough talk from the Bundesbank and the slightly overbought situation in the dollar and oversold situation in the mark has created a new outlook," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerishe Landesbank Girzentrale in New York.
The dollar fell to 1.8205 marks from 1.8395 at Thursday's close. It ended at 117.60 yen, off from 117.85.

The German central bank has been sounding warnings about inflation all week. On Thursday, hawkish remarks from Bundesbank Vice President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum fanned expectations it might boost short-term interest rates when it returns from summer recess Thursday.
Such a move would make mark-denominated investments more attractive compared with U.S. assets.
The dollar got little support from European markets, many of which were closed in observance of a religious holiday, Assumption Day.

"There is a whole lot going on here. I think the asset markets taking a dive certainly have not helped. A big holiday in Europe and thin markets certainly exaggerated the move," said Cynthia Cooley, a senior trader at United Gulf Bank of Bahrain in Boston.
The Dow industrials tumbled more than 247 points Friday, ending at 7,694.,66. The 30-year Treasury bond ended flat after trimming early losses of more than a point.
The dollar reversed overnight gains against the yen, which remained weak following Indonesia's de facto devaluation of its currency, the rupiah, Thursday.
Indonesia floated the rupiah under pressure from speculators, following similar actions by several neighboring countries in recent weeks. The currency hit another record low Friday.
Traders feared Japan might be compelled to weaken the yen to keep its exports competitive with other Pacific Rim nations.

"(The dollar) hasn't come off quite as much because of turbulence in the region," Cooley said. "Some would argue that the yen could become a regional safe-haven currency, but I think it's more likely that we'll see it weighs on (regional currencies) as a whole."
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.5065 Swiss francs from 1.5173 Thursday and to Canadian $1.3903 from C$1.3905.
